review_basis: Visually inspected each original Module 09 numbered WebP for this part, tracing its actual diagrams, numerical examples, decisions, and caveats. Scripts follow original visual reading order.
part_title: SageMaker Clarify — Evaluation, Explainability and Bias

scenes.title: SageMaker Clarify: foundation-model evaluation
scenes.narration: This slide evaluates a foundation model by following four large panels. Start with curated prompt data: representative questions, varied styles, difficult cases, and criteria for judging responses. Next, automated quality metrics assess useful properties, illustrated as relevance, coherence, groundedness, and potentially harmful content. Automated scores help at scale, but they do not replace judgment. The third panel adds human reviewers who consider accuracy, helpfulness, tone, and safety. The fourth combines those findings to decide whether the model is ready, should be improved, or should be replaced. Follow the customer support example at the bottom: realistic customer questions feed into automatic checks, then reviewers consider actual model answers, and the team decides whether to deploy. On the far right, note the distinction from bias evaluation, which examines unfair patterns, and explainability, which examines why a model produced an output. Quality evaluation asks how well the model performs on representative tasks. Neither a passing score nor a polished response proves every generated answer is correct.

scenes.title: SageMaker Clarify – Model Explainability
scenes.narration: The top row traces a loan approval explanation. First a trained model in SageMaker receives applicant inputs, including income, debt-to-income ratio, credit score, and employment length. SageMaker Clarify then calculates feature attribution for an individual prediction, and the final panel aggregates attributions across many predictions to provide global insight. The worked application below has income of seventy thousand dollars, debt-to-income ratio of zero point two eight, credit score seven hundred twenty, five years of employment, and eight accounts. The illustrated prediction is approve loan. In this particular explanation, credit score contributes plus zero point three five and income plus zero point two zero; debt-to-income ratio contributes minus zero point one eight. The bars explain the model's prediction in its selected attribution scale, not real-world causal effects. The global plot on the right uses average absolute attribution magnitude to compare overall importance across many applications. The two yellow callouts are essential: attribution is not causality, and Clarify is useful when the goal is understanding which inputs influenced predictions. Explanations do not by themselves establish fairness.

scenes.title: Detecting bias in datasets and predictions
scenes.narration: Follow the five numbered panels across the middle. Historical loan-application data in Amazon S3 may include group attributes such as age group, gender, or location. SageMaker Clarify analyzes the data and model predictions, then produces group-level bias and explainability reports. Human experts review the findings in their real-world context, change data or model design where appropriate, and reassess a model before deployment. The upper-right box separates pretraining dataset bias from posttraining prediction bias. The bottom example shows three groups with different illustrative positive prediction rates and false positive rates. Such differences are signals to investigate; a chart by itself cannot establish the reason, legal status, or appropriate remedy. A false positive rate asks how often a negative case is incorrectly predicted positive. Domain experts should check whether the groups, labels, sample sizes, and metrics are appropriate. The decision cue is to use Clarify to find potential disparities and support remediation, then re-evaluate rather than assume a monitoring report automatically makes a model fair.

scenes.title: Different kinds of biases (definitions)
scenes.narration: The slide introduces four named biases from left to right. Sampling bias occurs when the collected examples fail to represent the population where the model will be used. The hiring example trains mostly on one region and may not generalize to others. Measurement bias arises when a field is recorded inaccurately or inconsistently; the example is a crude one-to-five pain scale that under-represents some patient experiences. Observer bias happens when a human labeler's expectations influence the labels, such as treating equivalent content from groups differently. Confirmation bias occurs when an evaluator looks mainly for examples supporting an existing belief and ignores failures, shown in the last panel. Notice that the middle sections mention data labeling and SageMaker Ground Truth, while the final panel mentions Clarify for evaluation. These services can help organize labeling or detect disparities, but they cannot remove every human assumption. The exam cue is to identify where the problem starts: nonrepresentative sampling, faulty measurement, human labeling influence, or selective interpretation of evidence.
